paragraphs.text: Along the coasts of the Mediterranean, the remains of Roman harbours still stand in the waves, their piers battered by salt water for some two thousand years. In Rome itself, the Pantheon, completed in the second century AD, still carries the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Such survivals are all the more striking when set beside the record of modern construction. Many of the bridges, car parks and sea walls built during the twentieth century began to crack and crumble within fifty or a hundred years, and engineers today typically design new structures to last around a century. The contrast has prompted a simple but persistent question: what did Roman builders understand that their modern successors have overlooked?
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Part of the answer lies in the ingredients. Modern concrete is held together by Portland cement, a material patented in Britain in the early nineteenth century and made by heating limestone and clay in kilns to about 1,450°C. Roman builders instead combined lime with volcanic ash, the best of which was dug from deposits around the Bay of Naples, near the town of Pozzuoli. Their lime was produced at roughly 900°C, a far lower temperature, and the ash supplied silica and alumina that reacted with it to form a dense, stone-like binder. Into this paste workers packed fist-sized chunks of rock or broken brick, building up walls and foundations layer by layer rather than pouring a liquid mixture into moulds, as is common practice today.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For centuries, observers assumed that the harbour structures had simply been lucky, or that the calm waters of the Mediterranean had treated them unusually kindly. Seawater normally attacks concrete: salts seep into tiny pores and react with the cement, causing it to swell and split. Yet when a team led by the geologist Ines Varga examined cores drilled from an ancient pier, they found the opposite process at work. As seawater percolated through the material, it dissolved some of the volcanic ash and allowed new minerals to grow in the spaces left behind. Long, plate-shaped crystals had formed within the pores and cracks, interlocking like the fibres of a woven mat. Rather than weakening the concrete, the sea appeared to have been slowly reinforcing it, so that the oldest sections were in some respects stronger than when they were first built.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A second clue came from something earlier researchers had dismissed as a flaw. Roman concrete is dotted with small white lumps of lime, a few millimetres across, which were long blamed on careless mixing or poor-quality materials. Materials scientist Tomas Reyes and his colleagues argued instead that these lumps, known as lime clasts, were a by-product of 'hot mixing', in which builders added quicklime directly to the ash and water, generating intense heat. To test the idea, the team made samples using this method, deliberately cracked them and then allowed water to run through the gaps. Within two weeks the cracks had sealed completely: the water had dissolved calcium from the clasts, which then recrystallised as calcium carbonate and filled the openings. Identical samples made without the clasts continued to leak.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: None of this means that Roman concrete is simply superior. It is considerably weaker under compression than its modern equivalent, and it hardens slowly, sometimes over months, whereas contractors today expect a new floor slab to bear loads within days. Nor could it support the slender towers and long spans of contemporary architecture. These depend on steel bars embedded in the concrete to resist bending and stretching, and here lies a paradox. Steel gives modern structures much of their strength, but once moisture and salt reach it, the metal begins to rust. Because rust occupies more space than the original steel, it pushes outwards and breaks the surrounding concrete apart from within. Roman builders, who used no such reinforcement, never faced this particular form of decay.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Engineers are now trying to combine the strengths of both traditions. Few expect ancient recipes simply to replace modern ones. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, partly because of the fuel burned to reach such high kiln temperatures, so a mixture that needs less heat and lasts longer could bring considerable environmental benefits. Several laboratories are experimenting with recipes that add volcanic ash, or industrial waste with similar chemistry, to modern cement, and some are testing whether lime clasts could give new buildings the ability to repair their own cracks. The coastal engineer Marta Lindqvist believes Roman-style concrete may prove most valuable for sea walls and other marine structures, where corrosion is the greatest threat. She warns, however, that promising laboratory results do not guarantee success outdoors. 'The Romans had centuries to demonstrate that their concrete worked,' she says. 'We will need patience before we can claim the same for ours.'
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
The Secret of Roman Concrete

A. Along the coasts of the Mediterranean, the remains of Roman harbours still stand in the waves, their piers battered by salt water for some two thousand years. In Rome itself, the Pantheon, completed in the second century AD, still carries the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Such survivals are all the more striking when set beside the record of modern construction. Many of the bridges, car parks and sea walls built during the twentieth century began to crack and crumble within fifty or a hundred years, and engineers today typically design new structures to last around a century. The contrast has prompted a simple but persistent question: what did Roman builders understand that their modern successors have overlooked?

B. Part of the answer lies in the ingredients. Modern concrete is held together by Portland cement, a material patented in Britain in the early nineteenth century and made by heating limestone and clay in kilns to about 1,450°C. Roman builders instead combined lime with volcanic ash, the best of which was dug from deposits around the Bay of Naples, near the town of Pozzuoli. Their lime was produced at roughly 900°C, a far lower temperature, and the ash supplied silica and alumina that reacted with it to form a dense, stone-like binder. Into this paste workers packed fist-sized chunks of rock or broken brick, building up walls and foundations layer by layer rather than pouring a liquid mixture into moulds, as is common practice today.

C. For centuries, observers assumed that the harbour structures had simply been lucky, or that the calm waters of the Mediterranean had treated them unusually kindly. Seawater normally attacks concrete: salts seep into tiny pores and react with the cement, causing it to swell and split. Yet when a team led by the geologist Ines Varga examined cores drilled from an ancient pier, they found the opposite process at work. As seawater percolated through the material, it dissolved some of the volcanic ash and allowed new minerals to grow in the spaces left behind. Long, plate-shaped crystals had formed within the pores and cracks, interlocking like the fibres of a woven mat. Rather than weakening the concrete, the sea appeared to have been slowly reinforcing it, so that the oldest sections were in some respects stronger than when they were first built.

D. A second clue came from something earlier researchers had dismissed as a flaw. Roman concrete is dotted with small white lumps of lime, a few millimetres across, which were long blamed on careless mixing or poor-quality materials. Materials scientist Tomas Reyes and his colleagues argued instead that these lumps, known as lime clasts, were a by-product of 'hot mixing', in which builders added quicklime directly to the ash and water, generating intense heat. To test the idea, the team made samples using this method, deliberately cracked them and then allowed water to run through the gaps. Within two weeks the cracks had sealed completely: the water had dissolved calcium from the clasts, which then recrystallised as calcium carbonate and filled the openings. Identical samples made without the clasts continued to leak.

E. None of this means that Roman concrete is simply superior. It is considerably weaker under compression than its modern equivalent, and it hardens slowly, sometimes over months, whereas contractors today expect a new floor slab to bear loads within days. Nor could it support the slender towers and long spans of contemporary architecture. These depend on steel bars embedded in the concrete to resist bending and stretching, and here lies a paradox. Steel gives modern structures much of their strength, but once moisture and salt reach it, the metal begins to rust. Because rust occupies more space than the original steel, it pushes outwards and breaks the surrounding concrete apart from within. Roman builders, who used no such reinforcement, never faced this particular form of decay.

F. Engineers are now trying to combine the strengths of both traditions. Few expect ancient recipes simply to replace modern ones. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, partly because of the fuel burned to reach such high kiln temperatures, so a mixture that needs less heat and lasts longer could bring considerable environmental benefits. Several laboratories are experimenting with recipes that add volcanic ash, or industrial waste with similar chemistry, to modern cement, and some are testing whether lime clasts could give new buildings the ability to repair their own cracks. The coastal engineer Marta Lindqvist believes Roman-style concrete may prove most valuable for sea walls and other marine structures, where corrosion is the greatest threat. She warns, however, that promising laboratory results do not guarantee success outdoors. 'The Romans had centuries to demonstrate that their concrete worked,' she says. 'We will need patience before we can claim the same for ours.'
